blocks.title: Why caches work
blocks.text: A cache keeps recently or nearby used memory blocks close to the processor. Temporal locality means recently accessed data is likely to be used again, while spatial locality means addresses near a recent access are likely to be used soon.

blocks.title: Address fields
blocks.text: A cache interprets an address using an offset, an index, and a tag. The offset selects a byte within a block, the index selects a set, and the stored tag determines whether a line in that set contains the requested memory block.

blocks.title: Direct mapping
blocks.text: In a direct-mapped cache, each memory block can occupy exactly one cache line selected by the index. Lookup is simple, but two frequently used blocks with the same index repeatedly evict one another and cause conflict misses.

blocks.title: Set associativity
blocks.text: In a set-associative cache, the index selects a set containing several ways, and the requested block may occupy any way in that set. More ways can reduce conflict misses, but parallel tag comparisons increase hardware cost and may lengthen hit time.

blocks.title: Hit path
blocks.text: A cache hit occurs when a valid line in the selected set has a matching tag. The cache returns the requested bytes using the block offset, avoiding the longer latency of fetching the block from the next memory level.

blocks.title: Miss path
blocks.text: On a cache miss, the requested block is fetched from a lower memory level and placed in a selected line. If the victim line is dirty in a write-back cache, its modified contents must be written to the lower level before replacement.

blocks.title: Miss categories
blocks.text: A compulsory miss is the first access to a block. A capacity miss occurs when the working set exceeds total cache capacity. A conflict miss occurs when placement restrictions make blocks compete even though other cache lines are available.

blocks.title: Average memory access time
blocks.text: Average memory access time equals hit time plus miss rate multiplied by miss penalty. Lowering miss rate helps, but an optimization can still hurt overall performance if it increases hit time enough to outweigh the saved misses.
